section_summary: This section opens with correspondence between Stanford historian Thomas A. Bailey and the State Department concerning the 1912 Magdalena Bay controversy, the Lodge Resolution, and rumored Japanese land purchases in Baja California. Most of the section consists of confidential diplomatic, military, naval, consular, and Justice Department reports from 1931–1932 alleging that Japanese sampans and engineers were surveying the Mexican Pacific coast, the Gulf of California, Sonora, and Chihuahua. The reports are repeatedly described as unconfirmed or based on informants, but they prompted discreet inquiries by Ambassador J. Reuben Clark Jr. and assurances from Mexican officials. The section also contains public alarm about Japanese immigration and a translated anti-American article attributed to General Kiyokatsu Satō.

subfiles.title: Request for records concerning Magdalena Bay and the Lodge Resolution
subfiles.from: Thomas A. Bailey
subfiles.to: Tyler Dennett, Historical Adviser, Department of State
subfiles.about: Bailey requests unpublished correspondence concerning Japanese and Mexican denials of designs on Magdalena Bay.
subfiles.summary: Bailey explains that his study of Magdalena Bay and the Lodge Resolution repeatedly encounters references to denials by Japan and Mexico. Because the published Foreign Relations volumes omit the episode, he asks for copies of any written denials or related unpublished correspondence.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the 1912 Magdalena Bay rumors
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department reports that the Japanese and Mexican denials were public and oral rather than written diplomatic exchanges.
subfiles.summary: A file search found no written communications exchanged between the governments concerning the 1912 incident. Japan and Mexico issued statements to the press, and the Japanese Embassy, Foreign Office, and ambassador orally denied any Japanese government or corporate purchase at Magdalena Bay. Bailey is asked not to attribute the information to the Department.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about later applications of the Lodge Resolution
subfiles.from: Thomas A. Bailey
subfiles.about: Bailey asks whether the State Department invoked the Lodge Resolution against a rumored 1919 Japanese land purchase in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: Bailey cites New York Times reports that the Department warned a Los Angeles land company about selling its Baja California holdings to Japanese subjects. He requests confirmation and asks for other examples of the resolution's use.

subfiles.title: State Department account of applications of the Lodge Resolution
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department confirms several occasions when landowners were sent congressional documents expressing U.S. policy toward Japanese acquisitions in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms that in March 1919 it sent a Los Angeles company copies of Senate documents bearing on a reported sale to a Japanese entity. Similar material was sent to persons interested in land in southwestern Mexico and Sonora, including coal and colonization tracts. The examples are presented as illustrative rather than exhaustive, and Bailey is again asked not to cite the Department.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of State Department assistance
subfiles.from: Thomas A. Bailey
subfiles.about: Bailey thanks Hornbeck for the Magdalena Bay information and promises not to identify the Department as its source.
subfiles.summary: Bailey acknowledges Hornbeck's letters of January 17 and March 30. He calls the enclosed information valuable and confirms that the State Department will not be quoted or mentioned in his use of it.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs recommendation concerning the Japanese sampans
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: An internal note suggests instructing the vice consul to report reliable information bearing on the truth of the sampan rumors.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten note proposes follow-up reporting by the vice consul. It appears to concern allegations that purported fishing vessels were conducting surveys.

subfiles.title: Mexican Affairs comment on the sampan report
subfiles.from: Division of Mexican Affairs
subfiles.about: Mexican Affairs asks Hornbeck how much importance he attaches to the report and comments on the reporting officer.
subfiles.summary: The note seeks an assessment of the report's significance. Its final comment about the reporting officer is partly illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Japanese sampans cruising along the west coast of Mexico
subfiles.from: E. W. Eaton, American Vice Consul, Mazatlán
subfiles.about: Eaton reports suspicions that four Japanese sampans ostensibly engaged in pearl fishing were mapping the Mexican coast.
subfiles.summary: Four Japanese sampans led by Naotaro Kobayashi called at Mazatlán while proceeding north through the Gulf of California. Although Kobayashi claimed a pearl-fishing concession, observers saw no fishing equipment or pearls. Local rumor held that the vessels were visiting and charting coves, inlets, and harbors from Acapulco toward Guaymas, Baja California, and Ensenada.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate rumors concerning Japanese sampans
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: E. W. Eaton, American Vice Consul, Mazatlán
subfiles.about: The Department directs Eaton to report reliable evidence confirming or disproving the alleged coastal surveys.
subfiles.summary: The instruction summarizes Eaton's report that the sampans claimed to be pearl-fishing vessels but were rumored to be mapping the coast. Eaton is ordered to forward any reliable information bearing on the truth or falsity of those claims.

subfiles.title: File-number marker 894.20212/311
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: A marker records the decimal file number 894.20212/311.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only a file designation. No substantive communication is present.

subfiles.title: Justice Department report of Japanese engineers in Sonora
subfiles.from: William D. Mitchell, Attorney General
subfiles.about: The Attorney General forwards a report that thirty Japanese engineers landed at Guaymas and began topographical work in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: Mounted Customs Inspector T. B. Doolittle reportedly learned that thirty Japanese engineers landed at Guaymas around October 8, 1931, and mapped roads on the Sonora coast. Their official or commercial status was unknown. The Justice Department planned a U.S.-based investigation after the Navy requested more information.

subfiles.title: Navy request for investigation of Japanese engineers
subfiles.from: C. F. Adams, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Adams asks the Justice Department to obtain more information about Japanese survey activity in Sonora and the location of Caborca.
subfiles.summary: The Navy expresses interest in the reported activities of Japanese engineers in Sonora. It particularly requests identification of the surveyed areas and clarification of the reported town name “Cabosca,” which it had been unable to locate.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence memorandum on Japanese activities, first copy
subfiles.from: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: The memorandum compiles allegations of Japanese surveying and intelligence collection in Mexico, Alaska, Hawaii, and other strategic locations.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum begins with the report of thirty Japanese engineers operating from Guaymas and Caborca. It reviews earlier allegations involving Japanese charting, photography, scientific collecting, and naval personnel in Alaska and around Hawaii. It also cites suspicious sampans at Manzanillo, Mazatlán, and Guaymas, reported surveying near Washington State, and activities around the Caribbean approaches to the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence memorandum on Japanese activities, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: This is a second file copy of the memorandum compiling reports of Japanese reconnaissance along Mexico's coast and at other strategic points.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate repeats allegations concerning engineers in Sonora, Japanese vessels and photographers in the Aleutians, and sampans moving from Manzanillo to Guaymas. It also repeats reports from Hawaii, Washington State, Latin America, and the West Indies. Much of the information is secondhand and framed as an intelligence recapitulation rather than confirmed fact.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate Japanese activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: J. Reuben Clark Jr., American Ambassador to Mexico
subfiles.about: The Department sends Justice and Navy reports to Clark and asks for discreet investigation of alleged Japanese surveys.
subfiles.summary: Clark receives the Attorney General's report, the Navy communication, the State Department's reply, and the Naval Intelligence memorandum. He is asked to obtain information discreetly and may instruct west-coast consuls to report relevant Japanese activity. Consular reports are to be sent to both the Embassy and Department.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Attorney General concerning Japanese engineers
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges the Sonora report and asks to receive any additional evidence obtained from Doolittle.
subfiles.summary: The letter restates the allegation that thirty Japanese engineers landed at Guaymas and conducted topographical surveys. It notes the Justice Department's effort to question T. B. Doolittle further and requests any additional information developed.

subfiles.title: Follow-up report on Japanese sampans
subfiles.from: E. W. Eaton, American Vice Consul, Mazatlán
subfiles.about: Eaton reports additional but inconclusive evidence that the sampans photographed harbors and took soundings while traveling toward the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: Allison V. Armour reported encountering the sampans at Acapulco, Manzanillo, Mazatlán, and Guaymas without visible fishing gear. Fishermen from Puerto Vallarta and San Blas claimed that the Japanese took soundings, drew maps, and photographed the harbors. Mexican port officials regarded the expedition as legitimate fishing, but Eaton noted that its long and costly route to collect Kobayashi at Acapulco remained suspicious.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department
subfiles.to: Military, naval, State, and Commerce Department distribution list
subfiles.about: A standardized routing sheet lists offices eligible to receive the attached intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The form names War Department branches, the Office of Naval Intelligence, State Department divisions, and Commerce Department offices. No substantive intelligence is recorded on the page.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of report on Japanese marine activities near Guaymas
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 sends the attaché an Eighth Corps Area report on Japanese marine activity near Guaymas.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses a December 17 report concerning Japanese vessels in the vicinity of Guaymas. A State Department copy was supplied for information and filing.

subfiles.title: Statement on Japanese fishing boats at Guaymas
subfiles.from: L. B. Clapham, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: The report forwards Royal J. Swift's claim that Japanese boats at Guaymas were conducting government surveys rather than fishing.
subfiles.summary: Swift said the boats brought in no fish and that their leader appeared unusually educated for a fisherman. Local residents allegedly believed a Japanese government engineer was taking notes, making soundings, and visiting Magdalena Bay. The statement also mentions an unsuccessful request for land for a colony.

subfiles.title: Identification of Caborca and Japanese produce merchants
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 identifies the reported “Cabosca” as Caborca and supplies immigration details on three Japanese travelers to Culiacán.
subfiles.summary: An enclosed First Cavalry Division report identifies the Sonora locality as Caborca. Immigration records describe Ote Kamade, Matauahi Haruse, and Kemiire Shinazakd as Los Angeles produce merchants traveling briefly to Culiacán to buy tomatoes. The men were readmitted to the United States as lawfully domiciled aliens.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division report on Japanese engineers in Sonora
subfiles.from: William Nalle, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, First Cavalry Division
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Nalle forwards an unconfirmed report of thirty Japanese engineers in Sonora and a later landing of purported fishermen.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the engineer story through Justice agent R. H. Calvin, Inspector Doolittle, and informant Lewis Collins. It alleges that thirty engineers landed at Guaymas, dispersed through Sonora, and used surveying instruments. A separate rumor says a Japanese warship landed twelve to fifteen ostensible fishermen near El Rosario or La Paz.

subfiles.title: Initial G-2 transmittal on alleged Japanese activities
subfiles.from: War Department G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 sends reports and press material about alleged Japanese activities on Mexico's west coast for comment or confirmation.
subfiles.summary: The enclosures included a War Department memorandum based on Justice Department information and reports attributed to Otto Holstein. A translated article from the Mexico City newspaper La Prensa was also included. Copies went to Naval Intelligence and the State Department.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of additional Eighth Corps intelligence
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 sends a January 4 Eighth Corps Area summary of further allegations concerning Japanese activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The letter follows earlier communications of December 15, 17, and 24. It forwards the latest Eighth Corps Area report and notes that copies also went to Naval Intelligence and the State Department.

subfiles.title: Eighth Corps Area report on Japanese activities in Mexico
subfiles.from: Edwin B. Winans, Commanding General, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: The report compiles allegations about Japanese survey parties, vessels, petroleum shipments, and commercial inquiries in northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Informants claimed that more than thirty Japanese had worked between San Luis, El Mayor, and Port Isabel and that Japanese legation personnel obtained official papers for them. Other reports placed Japanese engineers around Caborca and nearby Gulf locations, while an alleged Japanese government adviser, Harold E. Palmer, traveled through Arizona. The report also records petroleum shipments toward Japan, Japanese and Chinese interest in Mexican nitrates, and speculation about the expulsion of Chinese residents from Sonora. Winans judged the claims unconfirmed but worthy of investigation outside his command's jurisdiction.

subfiles.title: Notice of War Department reports sent to the Military Attaché
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department informs the ambassador of additional War Department correspondence concerning Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to the previous January 15 mailing of reports. It identifies a January 13 War Department letter and a January 4 Eighth Corps Area report, as well as earlier December communications sent to the Embassy's military attaché.

subfiles.title: Forwarding of Justice Department report to Ambassador Clark
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwards a new Justice Department report containing additional information on alleged Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers back to the January 30 correspondence series and encloses the Justice Department's January 23 letter. A special agent's report accompanied it for the ambassador's confidential consideration.

subfiles.title: File-number marker 894.20212/316
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: A marker records the decimal file number 894.20212/316.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the file designation. It carries no substantive message.

subfiles.title: Clark telegram on discussions with Téllez and Calles
subfiles.from: J. Reuben Clark Jr., American Ambassador, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Clark reports that he raised the alleged Japanese surveys informally with Foreign Minister Téllez and General Calles.
subfiles.summary: Clark presented a memorandum on reported Japanese engineer landings at Guaymas, El Rosario, or La Paz while emphasizing that the United States could not vouch for the reports. He explained that trained Japanese near the border might present a sabotage risk in a future U.S.–Japanese conflict. Téllez promised an investigation and said Mexico would not align with Japan; Calles likewise promised inquiry and indicated benevolent neutrality toward the United States.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Clark's telegram, first copy
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: This paraphrase restates Clark's informal presentation to Mexican leaders concerning alleged Japanese surveys.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase records Clark's disclaimer that the border reports were unverified and his acknowledgment of Mexico's right to employ Japanese surveyors. It emphasizes American concern about possible sabotage and records promises of investigation and Mexican neutrality. The document resolves the ambiguous wording of the original telegram in favor of benevolent neutrality toward the United States.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Clark's telegram, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: A second, poorly reproduced copy paraphrases Clark's February 6 telegram.
subfiles.summary: Despite severe OCR corruption, the duplicate follows the same structure as the preceding paraphrase. It recounts the reports of Japanese engineers, Clark's warning about access to U.S. territory, and assurances from Mexican officials that they would investigate and not support Japan against the United States.

subfiles.title: Warning to President Hoover about Japanese residents in Mexico
subfiles.from: S. Weston Hastings
subfiles.about: Hastings warns that Japanese residents in Mexico could supposedly be mobilized for an attack across the U.S. border.
subfiles.summary: Hastings portrays Japanese ranchers in Mexico as numerous, militarily trained, mobile, and capable of threatening border oil fields. He urges stronger border defenses and weapons for civilian population centers. The letter also speculates that Mexican resentment over Texas and California could assist such an attack.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to S. Weston Hastings
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Hastings's warning about the Japanese population in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes that the White House referred Hastings's letter to it. Hamilton states only that the letter was read with interest and that the Department appreciated Hastings's courtesy.

subfiles.title: Notice of two further War Department communications
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises the ambassador that the Military Attaché received two new War Department reports on Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The War Department communications were dated February 4 and February 6 and transmitted reports from the Eighth Corps Area and First Cavalry Division. One enclosure duplicated a Justice Department special-agent report already sent to the ambassador.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Eighth Corps Area report on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: James Totten, for the Commanding General, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: The report corrects the location of Caborca and summarizes intelligence on Palmer, Japanese interests in Sonora, Tijuana rumors, and propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Manuel Sorola corrects “Cabosca” to Caborca, while a detailed inquiry portrays Harold E. Palmer as a legitimate educator and lecturer rather than a suspicious agent. Other informants allege a Japanese-operated silk mill at Álamos and identify a farmer named Tanaka as a Japanese government representative in Ciudad Obregón. A pseudonymous Tijuana source repeats rumors of Japanese espionage and a mass landing near Magdalena Bay. The report encloses a Carteles article titled “Why Japan Hates the United States.”

subfiles.title: G-2 letter transmitting supplementary reports
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 sends the attaché the January 18 Eighth Corps report and Manuel Sorola's investigation of Japanese engineers and fishermen.
subfiles.summary: The letter links land-survey engineers in western Sonora with purported fishermen exploring adjacent waters and notes claims that both groups came from a Japanese warship. It asks the attaché to clarify whether a Japanese engineer's safe-conduct letter came from the French minister or represented French commercial interests. The letter notes that Ambassador Clark already had Sorola's report.

subfiles.title: Translation of “Why Japan Hates the United States”
subfiles.from: B. N. Colon, translator; original attributed to General Kiyokatsu Satō
subfiles.about: The translation reproduces an anti-American chapter published in the Cuban magazine Carteles and attributed to a Japanese general.
subfiles.summary: The article depicts the United States as Japan's present enemy and lists grievances involving Commodore Perry, discrimination against Japanese immigrants, immigration exclusion, Qingdao, the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, Manchuria, and naval arms limits. It presents American policy as an assault on Japanese dignity, strategic interests, and sovereignty. The conclusion calls for preparation for a future Japanese-American war.

subfiles.title: G-2 transmittal of First Cavalry Division coastal report
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 transmits a First Cavalry Division report concerning Japanese coastal activity and a disputed safe-conduct letter.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed report largely duplicates information in Manuel Sorola's January 15 investigation. This version says that a Japanese engineer carried a recommendation from the Mexican Minister of Finance, not the French minister. G-2 highlights the discrepancy for possible clarification in Mexico City.

subfiles.title: Report of Japanese launches sounding the Gulf of California
subfiles.from: William Nalle, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, First Cavalry Division
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: The report alleges that launches from a Japanese warship systematically sounded the northern Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: An informant claimed that three gasoline launches worked from Guaymas to Camp Tornillo, especially around Tiburón Island, Puerto Libertad, Puerto Lobos, San Jorge Bay, and Adair Bay. Their zigzag movements and failure to land fish were interpreted as hydrographic surveying, with fuel reportedly trucked from San Luis. The report also mentions a Japanese engineer traveling under Mexican safe conduct and alleged propaganda among Sonora residents.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department
subfiles.to: Military, naval, State, and Commerce Department distribution list
subfiles.about: A standardized distribution form accompanies the intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The page lists potential military and civilian recipients. It contains no substantive report.

subfiles.title: G-2 transmittal concerning Japanese engineers near Pearson
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 forwards a report of fourteen Japanese engineers surveying northwest of Pearson, Chihuahua.
subfiles.summary: The letter presumes that the party may belong to the previously reported group of thirty engineers from Guaymas because Pearson lies near the Sonora boundary. It also notes an older allegation that Japanese army engineers mapped the Sierra Madre near Colonia Pacheco and northward toward the U.S. border.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department
subfiles.to: Military, naval, State, and Commerce Department distribution list
subfiles.about: A second standardized distribution form precedes related correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The form lists War Department branches and other federal offices. No narrative intelligence appears on the page.

subfiles.title: G-2 request to confirm the Pearson engineer report
subfiles.from: W. H. Simpson, Executive Officer, G-2
subfiles.to: Military Attaché, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: G-2 forwards the Pearson report and states that confirmation is being sought through the Eighth Corps Area.
subfiles.summary: Fourteen Japanese engineers were reportedly seen with levels and transits northwest of Pearson near the Sonora boundary. The letter connects them tentatively to the Guaymas group and recalls earlier alleged Japanese mapping near Sierra Pacheco. The Military Attaché is promised the results of further verification.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division report on surveyors near Pearson
subfiles.from: William Nalle, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, First Cavalry Division
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: An informant reports observing fourteen Japanese men using surveying instruments near Pearson and Colonia Pacheco.
subfiles.summary: The informant saw three groups using levels, transits, and a measuring wheel about eighteen miles northwest of Pearson. Mexican residents said the party had occupied the site since early January and was mapping the area. The informant also repeated a three-year-old story that Japanese army engineers had surveyed the Sierra Madre north toward the U.S. border, while cautioning that local Mormon settlers should be approached discreetly.
